decks.title: Current Electricity — Part 1: Ohm’s law and resistance
goals: Relate charge, current and potential difference, and use Q = It and V = W/Q
State Ohm’s law, describe its verification and find resistance from a V–I graph
Use R = ρl/A and explain how temperature and material affect resistance; describe superconductors

slides.heading: What keeps the charge moving?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a cell pushes charge round a circuit. How much flows, how hard it is pushed, and what holds it back are measured by **current**, **potential difference** and **resistance**.

visual.alt: Table of charge, current, potential difference and resistance with their symbols, units and measuring instruments

slides.narration: Namaste! When you switch on a study lamp, charge starts moving through its wires at once. In this part we measure how much charge flows each second, how strongly the cell pushes it, and how much the wire resists it. These three ideas, current, potential difference and resistance, are linked by a simple law named after Georg Ohm.

slides.heading: Charge and electric current
slides.body_md: Charge is carried in metals by **free electrons** (charge of one electron $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C). **Electric current** is the rate of flow of charge: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$. **1 ampere** = 1 coulomb passing a point each second. **Conventional current** flows from the **positive** terminal of the cell, through the outside circuit, to the **negative** terminal; electrons drift the opposite way.

visual.alt: Table of charge, time and the resulting current

slides.narration: Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point. One ampere means one coulomb every second. In a metal wire the charge is carried by free electrons, which drift from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal. By an old convention, though, we draw the current flowing the other way, out of the positive terminal and round to the negative.

slides.heading: Potential difference and resistance
slides.body_md: The **potential difference** between two points is the **work done per unit charge** in moving charge between them: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$; **1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb**. **Resistance** is the opposition a conductor offers to the flow of current: $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$; **1 ohm** is the resistance of a conductor that carries 1 A when the p.d. across it is 1 V.

nodes.label: Each coulomb gets V = W ÷ Q joules
Resistance R = V ÷ I opposes it

visual.alt: Flow from the work done by the cell to potential difference, current and resistance

slides.narration: A cell does work on each coulomb of charge it pushes. The work done per coulomb between two points is the potential difference, measured in volts, where one volt is one joule per coulomb. Every conductor holds back the flow a little. This opposition is its resistance, the potential difference divided by the current, measured in ohms.

slides.heading: Ohm’s law and its verification
slides.body_md: **Ohm’s law:** the current through a conductor is **directly proportional to the potential difference** across its ends, **provided its temperature and other physical conditions stay the same**: V ∝ I, or **V = IR**. **Verification:** connect the resistor with an **ammeter in series** and a **voltmeter in parallel**; change the current with the **rheostat**; record several pairs of V and I; the ratio V ÷ I stays constant.

slides.narration: Ohm’s law says the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, as long as its temperature stays the same. To check it, put an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the resistor. Turn the rheostat to change the current and note several pairs of readings. The voltage divided by the current comes out the same each time.

slides.heading: The V–I graph: finding R from the slope
slides.body_md: Plot **V on the y-axis** against **I on the x-axis**. For an **ohmic** conductor at constant temperature the points lie on a **straight line through the origin**, and **slope = V ÷ I = R**. For a **filament lamp** the graph **curves upwards**: as the filament heats up, its resistance rises, so V ÷ I grows.

visual.alt: Graph of potential difference against current. A manganin coil gives a straight line through the origin with slope six ohms. A torch bulb filament gives a curve that bends upwards, because its resistance rises as it heats up.
visual.caption: For an ohmic conductor the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin; its slope is the resistance.

slides.narration: Plot potential difference upwards and current along. A manganin coil gives a straight line through the origin, and the slope of that line is its resistance, here six ohms. A torch bulb filament gives a curve that bends upwards, because the filament gets hotter as the current grows, and a hotter metal has a higher resistance.

slides.heading: Worked example: using Ohm’s law
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The element of a soldering iron carries 0.5 A when connected to a 24 V transformer. (a) Find its resistance. (b) What current flows if it is connected to 18 V, its temperature staying the same?

**(a)** $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{24}{0.5} = 48$ Ω.

**(b)** $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{18}{48} = 0.375$ A.

visual.alt: Table of values in the soldering iron example

slides.narration: First find the resistance: twenty four volts divided by half an ampere gives forty eight ohms. If the temperature stays the same, the resistance stays the same, so at eighteen volts the current is eighteen divided by forty eight, which is three hundred and seventy five thousandths of an ampere. Always write the unit with each answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: Ohm’s law
slides.body_md: Find a resistance from a pair of readings.
slides.narration: Quick check. Resistance is the potential difference divided by the current.

slides.heading: Ohmic and non-ohmic conductors
slides.body_md: **Ohmic conductors** obey Ohm’s law: their V–I graph is a straight line through the origin (metal wires and alloys such as **nichrome, manganin, constantan** at constant temperature). **Non-ohmic conductors** do not: the V–I graph is a **curve**, or the current depends on which way it flows. Examples: a **filament lamp**, a **junction diode**, an **LED**, a **thermistor**, a **dilute acid** in a voltameter.

rows: Curves up (R rises as it heats)

visual.alt: Table comparing ohmic and non-ohmic conductors

slides.narration: A conductor that obeys Ohm’s law is called ohmic. Metal wires and alloys such as nichrome and manganin are ohmic, as long as their temperature does not change. Others are non-ohmic. A glowing lamp filament heats up, so its resistance rises. A diode lets current through easily in one direction only. Their graphs are not straight lines.

slides.heading: Factors affecting resistance
slides.body_md: The resistance of a wire depends on: (1) its **length** — $R \propto l$; (2) its **area of cross-section** — $R \propto \dfrac{1}{A}$ (thick wires have less resistance); (3) the **material**; (4) the **temperature** — for metals, R **increases** as temperature rises. Together: $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$, where $\rho$ is the **specific resistance (resistivity)** of the material.

slides.narration: A longer wire has more resistance, because the electrons must travel farther, colliding all the way. A thicker wire has less resistance, because it offers more room for the flow. Double the length and the resistance doubles; double the area and it halves. Resistance also depends on the material and, for metals, rises with temperature.

slides.heading: Worked example: specific resistance
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A coil for a hot-plate is wound from 5 m of nichrome wire of cross-sectional area $0.25 \times 10^{-6}$ m². Specific resistance of nichrome $= 1.1 \times 10^{-6}$ Ω m. Find (a) the resistance of the coil, (b) the length needed for a 33 Ω coil.

**(a)** $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.1 \times 10^{-6} \times 5}{0.25 \times 10^{-6}} = 22$ Ω.

**(b)** $l = \dfrac{RA}{\rho} = \dfrac{33 \times 0.25 \times 10^{-6}}{1.1 \times 10^{-6}} = 7.5$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the nichrome hot-plate example

slides.narration: Resistance equals specific resistance times length divided by area. Five metres of this nichrome wire gives twenty two ohms. For thirty three ohms, rearrange the formula: length equals resistance times area divided by specific resistance, which gives seven and a half metres. Notice that the powers of ten cancel neatly when you write the area in square metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: thickness of a wire
slides.body_md: Predict how resistance changes with the diameter of a wire.
slides.narration: Quick check. Area depends on the square of the diameter, and resistance is inversely proportional to area.

slides.heading: Specific resistance, temperature and superconductors
slides.body_md: **Specific resistance** $\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l}$ is the resistance of a wire of **unit length and unit area of cross-section**; SI unit **ohm metre (Ω m)**. It depends only on the **material** and its **temperature**, not on the wire’s size. **Metals:** resistance rises with temperature. **Semiconductors** (germanium, silicon): resistance falls as they warm. **Superconductors:** below a **critical temperature** their resistance becomes **zero** (mercury, below about 4.2 K).

visual.alt: Table of specific resistances of four materials and their uses

slides.narration: Specific resistance belongs to the material, not to the particular wire. Copper and aluminium have very low values, so they make good connecting wires. Alloys such as nichrome have high values, so they make good heating elements. Heating a metal raises its resistance. Cooling some materials far enough makes their resistance vanish completely. These are superconductors.

slides.heading: Quick check: superconductors
slides.body_md: Recall what happens to a superconductor below its critical temperature.
slides.narration: Quick check. Below the critical temperature, a superconductor has no resistance at all.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: I = Q ÷ t (ampere); V = W ÷ Q (volt); R = V ÷ I (ohm).
Ohm’s law: V ∝ I at constant temperature, so V = IR; slope of the V–I graph = R.
Ohmic: metals and alloys at constant temperature; non-ohmic: filament lamp, diode, thermistor.
R = ρl ÷ A: R grows with length, falls with area; ρ depends on material and temperature only.
Superconductors have zero resistance below a critical temperature.

rows: Any one of V, I, R
Resistance or length of a wire

visual.alt: Summary table of the three formulae of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Current is charge per second, potential difference is work per coulomb, and resistance is potential difference divided by current. Ohm’s law says that, at a steady temperature, current is proportional to potential difference. A wire’s resistance grows with its length, falls with its thickness, and depends on its material and temperature.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Always add “provided the temperature remains the same” when stating Ohm’s law.
Convert mm² to m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²) before using R = ρl ÷ A.
When a wire is stretched, its length rises and its area falls: R rises by the square of the stretch factor.
Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel — say so in every circuit description.

rows: With V on the y-axis, slope = R
Resistivity changes when the wire is cut
Only R changes; ρ stays the same

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. When you state Ohm’s law, always add the condition that the temperature stays the same. Change square millimetres into square metres before using the resistivity formula. Remember that cutting a wire changes its resistance but not its specific resistance. And in every circuit, place the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel.

decks.title: Current Electricity — Part 2: Cells and combinations of resistors
goals: Distinguish the e.m.f. of a cell from its terminal voltage
Use E = I(R + r) and V = E − Ir
Derive and use the equivalent resistance of resistors in series and in parallel
Find currents and potential differences in a simple series–parallel network

slides.heading: Inside the cell, and many paths
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a cell is not a perfect source: some of its push is used up inside it. And real circuits join resistors **one after another** or **side by side**.

rows: Why does a torch dim as its cells age?
Why do fairy lights go dark together?
Why do room lamps work independently?
How much current does the battery give?

visual.alt: Table of everyday questions and the idea each one uses

slides.narration: In this part we look inside the cell itself and find that some of its push is lost before the charge even leaves it. Then we join resistors in two ways: one after another, in series, and side by side, in parallel. With these ideas you can work out the current and the voltage in any simple circuit.

slides.heading: E.m.f. and terminal voltage
slides.body_md: **Electromotive force (e.m.f.), E:** the work done by the cell in moving a unit positive charge round the **whole circuit, including the cell**; it equals the p.d. across the terminals **when no current is drawn** (open circuit). **Terminal voltage, V:** the p.d. across the terminals **when the cell supplies current**. Because the cell has **internal resistance r**, part of the e.m.f. (the **lost volts, Ir**) is used inside it, so **V < E** while current flows.

rows: Less than E; falls as I rises

visual.alt: Table comparing the electromotive force and the terminal voltage of a cell

slides.narration: The electromotive force of a cell is the total work it does on each unit of charge sent round the circuit. You read it with a good voltmeter when the cell is not supplying current. Once current flows, some energy is used up inside the cell, so the voltage across its terminals, the terminal voltage, is smaller than the electromotive force.

slides.heading: Internal resistance in a circuit
slides.body_md: The cell behaves like an ideal e.m.f. E in series with a small **internal resistance r**. The current is $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}$, so $E = I(R + r) = IR + Ir$, that is **e.m.f. = terminal voltage + lost volts**, $V = E - Ir$. Internal resistance **increases** with the distance between the electrodes and the concentration of the electrolyte, and **decreases** with a larger area of electrodes in the electrolyte and a higher temperature.

slides.narration: Think of a real cell as a perfect source with a small resistor hidden inside it. The current is the electromotive force divided by the total resistance, outside plus inside. The push used inside is the current times the internal resistance, called the lost volts. What remains appears across the terminals. In the figure, three volts gives one ampere, and two and a half volts reach the terminals.

slides.heading: Worked example: finding internal resistance
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A battery reads 6 V on a high-resistance voltmeter when nothing else is connected. When a 5 Ω lamp is connected across it, the voltmeter reads 5 V. Find (a) the current, (b) the lost volts, (c) the internal resistance.

**(a)** $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{5}{5} = 1$ A.

**(b)** Lost volts $= E - V = 6 - 5 = 1$ V.

**(c)** $r = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1$ Ω.

visual.alt: Table of the readings and results in the internal resistance example

slides.narration: With nothing connected, the voltmeter reads the electromotive force, six volts. With the lamp on, it reads the terminal voltage, five volts. The current through the five ohm lamp is one ampere. The missing one volt was used inside the battery, so the internal resistance is one volt divided by one ampere, which is one ohm.

slides.heading: Quick check: e.m.f. and internal resistance
slides.body_md: Find the current from a cell with internal resistance.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the electromotive force by the external and internal resistances added together.

slides.heading: Terminal voltage falls as more current is drawn
slides.body_md: Since $V = E - Ir$, a graph of terminal voltage against current is a **straight line falling from E**. Its **intercept on the V-axis is the e.m.f.**, and it falls by **r volts for every ampere** drawn. A heavy load (small R, large I) makes the terminal voltage drop most — which is why headlights dim while a car’s starter motor is running.

functions.label: V = E − Ir (E = 3 V, r = 0.5 Ω)

visual.alt: Graph of terminal voltage against the current drawn from a cell of electromotive force three volts and internal resistance half an ohm. The line starts at three volts when no current flows and falls by half a volt for every ampere drawn.
visual.caption: Terminal p.d. falls as more current is drawn; the intercept is the e.m.f. and the fall per ampere is r.

slides.narration: The more current you draw, the more volts are lost inside the cell. So the terminal voltage falls in a straight line as the current rises. Where the line meets the voltage axis, no current flows, and the reading is the electromotive force. The steepness of the line tells you the internal resistance.

slides.heading: Resistors in series
slides.body_md: In **series**, resistors are joined **end to end**, so the **same current I** flows through each, and the p.d.s add: $V = V_{1} + V_{2} + V_{3}$. Using $V = IR$: $IR_{s} = IR_{1} + IR_{2} + IR_{3}$, so $R_{s} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3}$. The equivalent resistance is **more than the largest** resistor. If one part breaks, the whole circuit stops.

slides.narration: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current passes through every resistor. The battery voltage is shared out, and the biggest share goes to the biggest resistor. Since each share equals the current times that resistance, the equivalent resistance is simply the sum. In the figure, two, four and six ohms make twelve ohms.

slides.heading: Resistors in parallel
slides.body_md: In **parallel**, each resistor is connected **across the same two points**, so the **same p.d. V** is across each, and the currents add: $I = I_{1} + I_{2} + I_{3}$. Using $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$: $\dfrac{1}{R_{p}} = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{3}}$. The equivalent resistance is **less than the smallest** resistor. For two resistors, $R_{p} = \dfrac{R_{1}R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}$.

slides.heading: Worked example: series and parallel
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 12 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel across a 6 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Find the equivalent resistance and the current from the supply in each case.

**(a)** $R_{s} = 12 + 4 = 16$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{6}{16} = 0.375$ A.

**(b)** $R_{p} = \dfrac{12 \times 4}{12 + 4} = 3$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2$ A.

visual.alt: Table comparing the series and parallel results for the twelve ohm and four ohm resistors

slides.narration: In series, simply add: twelve plus four is sixteen ohms, and six volts drives a small current. In parallel, use product over sum: forty eight divided by sixteen gives three ohms, less than either resistor, so the same supply drives a much bigger current of two amperes. Parallel connection always draws more current from the supply.

slides.heading: A simple network
slides.body_md: **Method for a series–parallel network:** (1) replace each parallel group by its equivalent; (2) add the series parts, **including the internal resistance**; (3) find the total current from the e.m.f.; (4) work back: p.d. across each part with V = IR, then the current in each parallel branch. In the figure: 6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω = 2 Ω; total 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 Ω; I = 9 ÷ 5 = 1.8 A.

slides.heading: Worked example: currents in a network
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For the network in the figure (E = 9 V, r = 1 Ω, 2 Ω in series with 6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω), find the p.d. across the parallel pair, the current in each branch, and the terminal voltage.

**Parallel pair:** $\dfrac{6 \times 3}{6 + 3} = 2$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{9}{2 + 2 + 1} = 1.8$ A.

**p.d. across the pair:** $1.8 \times 2 = 3.6$ V.

**Branches:** $\dfrac{3.6}{6} = 0.6$ A and $\dfrac{3.6}{3} = 1.2$ A (sum 1.8 A ✓).

**Terminal voltage:** $9 - 1.8 \times 1 = 7.2$ V.

notes.title: Current Electricity — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Charge, current, potential difference and resistance
sections.body_md:
- **Current** is the rate of flow of charge: $I = Q/t$; unit **ampere** (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). Charge of an electron $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C; number of electrons $n = Q/e$.
- **Conventional current** flows from + to − in the outside circuit; electrons drift from − to +.
- **Potential difference** between two points = work done per unit charge moved between them: $V = W/Q$; **1 V = 1 J C⁻¹**.
- **Resistance** = opposition to current: $R = V/I$; **1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹**.
- **Ammeter**: low resistance, joined **in series**. **Voltmeter**: high resistance, joined **in parallel**.

key_terms.definition_md: The amount of charge flowing through a cross-section of a conductor in one second.
The work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point of a circuit to another.
The opposition a conductor offers to the flow of charge through it, measured as V divided by I.

visual.alt: Table of current, potential difference and resistance with units and meters

sections.heading: 2. Ohm’s law; ohmic and non-ohmic conductors
sections.body_md:
**Ohm’s law:** the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across its ends, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain unchanged: $V = IR$.

**Verification:** cell, key, rheostat, ammeter and the resistor in series; voltmeter across the resistor. Vary the current with the rheostat; for each setting record V and I. V ÷ I is constant, and the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin with **slope = R**.

**Ohmic conductors:** metals and alloys at constant temperature. **Non-ohmic:** filament lamp (graph curves as R rises with temperature), junction diode, LED, thermistor, electrolytes.

key_terms.definition_md: A conductor whose V–I graph is a straight line through the origin, so that its resistance does not depend on the current.
A conductor that does not obey Ohm’s law; its V–I graph is not a straight line through the origin.

visual.alt: Table of three conductors and whether they obey Ohm’s law

sections.heading: 3. Factors affecting resistance; specific resistance
sections.body_md:
- $R \propto l$ (longer, more resistance); $R \propto 1/A$ (thicker, less resistance); depends on **material** and **temperature**.
- $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$; **specific resistance (resistivity)** $\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l}$, the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section; unit **Ω m**.
- $\rho$ depends on the **material and temperature only**, not on length or area.
- Area of a round wire $A = \pi d^{2}/4$: halving the diameter makes R four times.
- Stretching a wire to n times its length (volume constant) makes its area 1/n times, so R becomes $n^{2}$ times.
- Copper and aluminium (low ρ): connecting wires and cables. Nichrome (high ρ, high melting point): heating elements. Manganin, constantan (resistance hardly changes with temperature): standard resistors.

key_terms.definition_md: The resistance of a conductor of the material having unit length and unit area of cross-section; also called resistivity.

visual.alt: Table of the effect of changes in a wire on its resistance and specific resistance

sections.heading: 4. Temperature, semiconductors and superconductors
sections.body_md:
- **Metals:** resistance increases with rise in temperature (the ions vibrate more and impede the electrons).
- **Alloys** (manganin, constantan): resistance changes very little with temperature.
- **Semiconductors** (silicon, germanium) and thermistors: resistance **decreases** as temperature rises.
- **Superconductors:** materials whose resistance becomes **zero** below a **critical temperature**; first seen in mercury below about 4.2 K. A current in a superconducting loop produces no heat, so it can flow without loss.

key_terms.definition_md: A material whose electrical resistance becomes zero when it is cooled below its critical temperature.
The temperature below which a material becomes superconducting.

visual.alt: Table of how resistance changes with temperature for three kinds of material

sections.heading: 5. E.m.f., internal resistance and terminal voltage
sections.body_md:
- **E.m.f. (E):** work done by the cell per unit positive charge in carrying it round the complete circuit, including the cell; equals the terminal p.d. on **open circuit**.
- **Terminal voltage (V):** p.d. across the terminals while the cell supplies current; $V = E - Ir$, so $V < E$.
- **Internal resistance (r):** resistance of the electrolyte (and electrodes) inside the cell. It **increases** with the separation of the electrodes and the concentration of the electrolyte; it **decreases** with a larger electrode area in the electrolyte and a higher temperature.
- $E = I(R + r)$; **lost volts** = $Ir$.

key_terms.definition_md: The energy supplied by a cell to each unit of charge driven round the whole circuit; it is the terminal voltage when no current is drawn.
The resistance offered by the electrolyte inside a cell to the flow of current through the cell.
The potential difference across the terminals of a cell while it is supplying current.

visual.alt: Table of terminal readings of a cell in three situations

sections.heading: 6. Resistors in series and in parallel; networks
sections.body_md:
**Series:** same current through each; $V = V_{1} + V_{2} + V_{3}$, so $R_{s} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3}$; $R_{s}$ is greater than the largest resistor; one break stops the whole circuit.

**Parallel:** same p.d. across each; $I = I_{1} + I_{2} + I_{3}$, so $\dfrac{1}{R_{p}} = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{3}}$; $R_{p}$ is less than the smallest; branches work independently. For n equal resistors R: series $nR$, parallel $R/n$.

**Networks:** reduce each parallel group, add series parts and r, find the main current, then work back with V = IR.

key_terms.definition_md: The single resistance that would draw the same current from the same source as a combination of resistors.

visual.alt: Table comparing series and parallel connections

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Leaving out “at constant temperature” from Ohm’s law.
- Forgetting to convert mm² to m² in R = ρl ÷ A.
- Saying specific resistance changes when a wire is cut or stretched.
- Ignoring the internal resistance when it is given.
- Forgetting to invert 1/Rp.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Calculations: formula (1), substitution with units (1), answer with unit (1).
- Laws: the statement with its condition.
- Derivations: state what is common to each resistor, write the equations, combine them.

questions.stem_md: While a hair dryer runs for 1 minute 15 seconds, a charge of 90 C flows through its heating coil. The current in the coil is:

the current through the filament stays the same at every voltage
the filament gets hotter, and the resistance of a metal rises with temperature

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Ohm’s law. Name one conductor that obeys it and one that does not. [3]

(b) A student records these readings for a coil: V = 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 V with I = 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 A. (i) Find the resistance of the coil. (ii) What current flows at 7.5 V? (iii) What p.d. is needed for a current of 2 A? [3]

(c) The filament of a torch bulb gives a V–I graph that is not a straight line. (i) Describe the shape of the graph. (ii) Explain it. (iii) Is the filament ohmic? (iv) Why must the condition of constant temperature be part of Ohm’s law? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Provided its temperature and physical state do not change, a conductor carries a current that is directly proportional to the p.d. across its ends. Ohmic: a manganin (or constantan) wire. Non-ohmic: a junction diode (or a filament lamp).

(b) (i) $R = \dfrac{1.5}{0.25} = 6$ Ω (the other pairs give the same ratio). (ii) $I = \dfrac{7.5}{6} = 1.25$ A. (iii) $V = 2 \times 6 = 12$ V.

(c) (i) With V on the y-axis, the graph curves upwards, getting steeper as the current grows. (ii) A larger current heats the filament more, and its resistance rises with temperature, so V ÷ I increases. (iii) No, it is non-ohmic. (iv) The resistance of a metal changes with temperature, so V ÷ I stays constant only if the temperature is kept the same.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State three factors on which the resistance of a metal wire depends, and say how it depends on each. [3]

(b) The heating coil of an immersion rod uses 1.5 m of alloy wire of cross-sectional area 0.3 mm²; the specific resistance of the alloy is $1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ Ω m. (i) Find the resistance of the coil. (ii) Find the current when 3 V is applied in a test. (iii) What length of the same wire would have a resistance of 20 Ω? [3]

(c) (i) What is a superconductor? (ii) Name the element in which superconductivity was first observed. (iii) State one advantage of superconducting power cables. (iv) How does the resistance of a silicon chip change when it is warmed? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Length: R is directly proportional to it. Area of cross-section: R is inversely proportional to it. Temperature: for a metal, R increases as it rises. (The material also decides R through its specific resistance.)

(b) (i) $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.5}{0.3 \times 10^{-6}} = 5$ Ω. (ii) $I = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$ A. (iii) $l = \dfrac{20 \times 0.3 \times 10^{-6}}{1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 6$ m.

(c) (i) A material whose resistance falls to zero below a critical temperature. (ii) Mercury (below about 4.2 K). (iii) No energy is wasted as heat in the cable. (iv) It decreases, since silicon is a semiconductor.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the e.m.f. of a cell and its internal resistance. State one factor that increases the internal resistance. [3]

(b) A cell of e.m.f. 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is joined to a 3.5 Ω resistor. Calculate (i) the current, (ii) the terminal voltage and (iii) the lost volts. [3]

(c) A voltmeter across a dry cell reads 1.5 V with the key open. When the key is closed so that the cell drives current through a 2 Ω resistor, the voltmeter reads 1.2 V. (i) Find the current. (ii) Find the internal resistance. (iii) Why does the reading fall when the key is closed? (iv) What would the voltmeter read if the 2 Ω resistor were replaced by a much larger one? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) E.m.f.: the work done by the cell per unit positive charge in taking it round the complete circuit, cell included (the terminal p.d. on open circuit). Internal resistance: the opposition of the electrolyte inside the cell to the current. It increases if the electrodes are farther apart (or the electrolyte is more concentrated, or the electrode area in the electrolyte is smaller).

(b) (i) $I = \dfrac{2}{3.5 + 0.5} = 0.5$ A. (ii) $V = 0.5 \times 3.5 = 1.75$ V. (iii) $Ir = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25$ V.

(c) (i) $I = \dfrac{1.2}{2} = 0.6$ A. (ii) $r = \dfrac{1.5 - 1.2}{0.6} = 0.5$ Ω. (iii) Current now flows through the internal resistance and 0.3 V is lost inside the cell. (iv) Nearly 1.5 V, because the current, and so Ir, becomes very small.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Three resistors $R_{1}$, $R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$ are connected in series across a battery. Derive an expression for their equivalent resistance. [3]

(b) Resistors of 4 Ω, 8 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in series across a 6 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Find (i) the equivalent resistance, (ii) the current and (iii) the p.d. across each resistor. [3]

(c) The same three resistors are now connected in parallel across the same supply. Find (i) the current in each resistor, (ii) the total current and (iii) the equivalent resistance. (iv) State one advantage of connecting household lamps in this way. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The same current I flows through each resistor, and the supply p.d. is shared: $V = V_{1} + V_{2} + V_{3} = IR_{1} + IR_{2} + IR_{3}$. For the equivalent resistor $V = IR_{s}$, so $IR_{s} = I(R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3})$ and $R_{s} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3}$.

(b) (i) $4 + 8 + 12 = 24$ Ω. (ii) $I = \dfrac{6}{24} = 0.25$ A. (iii) $0.25 \times 4 = 1$ V, $0.25 \times 8 = 2$ V, $0.25 \times 12 = 3$ V.

(c) (i) $\dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5$ A, $\dfrac{6}{8} = 0.75$ A, $\dfrac{6}{12} = 0.5$ A. (ii) $1.5 + 0.75 + 0.5 = 2.75$ A. (iii) $R_{p} = \dfrac{6}{2.75} \approx 2.18$ Ω. (iv) Each lamp gets the full mains voltage and can be switched on or off without affecting the others.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Derive the expression for the equivalent resistance of two resistors connected in parallel. [3]

(b) A battery of e.m.f. 6 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω is connected to a 1.6 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 4 Ω and 12 Ω. Find (i) the equivalent resistance of the pair, (ii) the current drawn from the battery and (iii) the terminal voltage. [3]

(c) (i) Find the p.d. across the parallel pair. (ii) Find the current in the 4 Ω and the 12 Ω resistors. (iii) The 12 Ω resistor is now removed. Find the new current from the battery. (iv) Does the terminal voltage rise or fall when the 12 Ω resistor is removed? Give a reason. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Both resistors have the same p.d. V; the currents add: $I = I_{1} + I_{2} = \dfrac{V}{R_{1}} + \dfrac{V}{R_{2}}$. For the equivalent resistor $I = \dfrac{V}{R_{p}}$, so $\dfrac{1}{R_{p}} = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}$, that is $R_{p} = \dfrac{R_{1}R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}$.

(b) (i) $\dfrac{4 \times 12}{4 + 12} = 3$ Ω. (ii) $I = \dfrac{6}{0.4 + 1.6 + 3} = 1.2$ A. (iii) $V = 6 - 1.2 \times 0.4 = 5.52$ V.

(c) (i) $1.2 \times 3 = 3.6$ V. (ii) $\dfrac{3.6}{4} = 0.9$ A and $\dfrac{3.6}{12} = 0.3$ A. (iii) Total resistance $0.4 + 1.6 + 4 = 6$ Ω, so $I = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1$ A. (iv) It rises (to $6 - 1 \times 0.4 = 5.6$ V), because a smaller current means smaller lost volts.
